stem: which Upanishad contains the great saying (mahavakya) "prajnanam brahma," "consciousness is Brahman"?
why: "prajnanam brahma" closes the Aitareya Upanishad of the Rig Veda (3.3); the Chandogya's great saying is "tat tvam asi," and the Mandukya's is "ayam atma brahma."

es.stem: ¿qué Upanishad contiene la gran sentencia (mahavakya) "prajnanam brahma", "la conciencia es Brahman"?
es.why: "prajnanam brahma" cierra la Aitareya Upanishad del Rig Veda (3.3); la gran sentencia de la Chandogya es "tat tvam asi", y la de la Mandukya, "ayam atma brahma".

stem: in the Chandogya Upanishad (6.1.4), Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu that by knowing one lump of clay, everything made of clay is known. what point is he making?
options: the world was shaped by the gods as a potter shapes clay
knowing many objects one at a time adds up to knowing all
pots differ only in name; the clay alone is what is real
the clay changes its true nature each time it is shaped
why: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.4: what is made of clay is only a change of name taken up in speech, and the truth is just clay; in the same way, knowing Being, the one source, everything is known.

es.stem: en la Chandogya Upanishad (6.1.4), Uddalaka le dice a su hijo Shvetaketu que al conocer un solo terrón de barro se conoce todo lo hecho de barro. ¿qué quiere mostrar?
options: los dioses dieron forma al mundo como un alfarero al barro
conocer muchas cosas una por una suma hasta conocerlo todo
las vasijas difieren solo en el nombre; lo real es el barro
el barro cambia su verdadera naturaleza cada vez que se moldea
es.why: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.4: lo hecho de barro es solo un cambio de nombre que se toma en el habla, y la verdad es solo barro; del mismo modo, conociendo el Ser, la única fuente, se conoce todo.

stem: in the Chandogya Upanishad (8.9), why does Indra turn back to Prajapati after being taught that the self is the body seen reflected in water?
options: he forgot the teaching on his way home and had to hear it again
he saw that such a self would decay and die with the body
Virochana challenged him to a debate that he could not win
the gods refused to accept him as king until he learned more
why: Chandogya Upanishad 8.9.1: Indra reasons that if the self were the reflected body, it would be blind when the body is blind and perish when it perishes, so he returns; Virochana takes the body as the self and goes home content.

es.stem: en la Chandogya Upanishad (8.9), ¿por qué Indra vuelve con Prajapati después de que le enseñaron que el ser es el cuerpo reflejado en el agua?
options: olvidó la enseñanza camino a casa y tuvo que oírla de nuevo
vio que ese ser se deterioraría y moriría junto con el cuerpo
Virochana lo desafió a un debate que él no podía ganar
los dioses no lo aceptaban como rey hasta que aprendiera más
es.why: Chandogya Upanishad 8.9.1: Indra razona que si el ser fuera el cuerpo reflejado, quedaría ciego cuando el cuerpo está ciego y perecería cuando el cuerpo perece, así que regresa; Virochana toma el cuerpo como el ser y se va contento.

stem: at King Janaka's court in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, which woman questions Yajnavalkya about what everything is "woven" on?
why: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.6 and 3.8: Gargi Vachaknavi asks on what water, wind and every world are woven, and later returns with her "two arrows"; Maitreyi talks with Yajnavalkya at home, not at court (2.4).

es.stem: en la corte del rey Janaka, en la Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, ¿qué mujer le pregunta a Yajnavalkya sobre qué está "tejido" todo?
es.why: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.6 y 3.8: Gargi Vachaknavi pregunta sobre qué están tejidos el agua, el viento y cada mundo, y luego vuelve con sus "dos flechas"; Maitreyi habla con Yajnavalkya en casa, no en la corte (2.4).

stem: in the Taittiriya Upanishad (2.1–2.5), which is the innermost of the five sheaths (koshas) of the self?
why: Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1–2.5 moves inward from the self made of food through breath, mind and understanding to the self made of bliss (anandamaya).

es.stem: en la Taittiriya Upanishad (2.1–2.5), ¿cuál es la más interior de las cinco envolturas (koshas) del ser?
es.why: Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1–2.5 va hacia adentro, del ser hecho de alimento, pasando por el aliento, la mente y el entendimiento, hasta el ser hecho de dicha (anandamaya).

stem: a scholar has mastered the four Vedas, phonetics, grammar and ritual, but has not come to know the imperishable. in the Mundaka Upanishad's terms (1.1.4–5), what kind of knowledge does he have?
why: Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.4–5 counts the four Vedas and their auxiliary sciences as the lower knowledge (apara vidya); the higher (para) is that by which the imperishable is grasped.

es.stem: un erudito domina los cuatro Vedas, la fonética, la gramática y el ritual, pero no ha llegado a conocer lo imperecedero. en los términos de la Mundaka Upanishad (1.1.4–5), ¿qué clase de conocimiento tiene?
options: brahma vidya, el conocimiento de Brahman
atma vidya, el conocimiento del ser
es.why: Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.4–5 cuenta los cuatro Vedas y sus ciencias auxiliares como el conocimiento inferior (apara vidya); el superior (para) es aquel por el que se capta lo imperecedero.

stem: in the Mundaka Upanishad (3.1.1–2), two birds sit on one tree: one eats the fruit, the other only watches. what do the two birds stand for, and how does the eating bird become free of grief?
why: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.1–2 (also Rig Veda 1.164.20 and Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4.6–7): the bird sunk on the tree grieves in its helplessness; when it sees the other, the Lord, and his greatness, its grief departs. Advaita reads the seeing as recognizing oneness; Dvaita and Vishishtadvaita read it as turning to a Lord distinct from the self.

rubric.point: identifies the eating bird as the one who tastes the fruits of action, sweet and bitter: the individual self (jiva). Shankara's alternative reading, in which the eater is the mind or intellect (sattva, buddhi), also counts.
identifies the watching bird as the one who does not eat and only looks on: the Lord or supreme self (most readings), or the self as pure witness (Shankara's alternative reading). both count.

says the eating bird is freed from grief when it sees the other bird, the Lord, and his greatness. either reading counts: recognizing its identity with it (Advaita) or turning to the Lord in dependence, distinct from him (Dvaita, Vishishtadvaita). freedom by eating better fruit does not count.
mentions that the tree stands for the body or the world.

es.stem: en la Mundaka Upanishad (3.1.1–2), dos pájaros están en un mismo árbol: uno come el fruto y el otro solo mira. ¿qué representan los dos pájaros, y cómo se libra de la pena el pájaro que come?
es.why: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.1–2 (también Rig Veda 1.164.20 y Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4.6–7): el pájaro hundido en el árbol se aflige en su impotencia; cuando ve al otro, el Señor, y su grandeza, su pena se va. El Advaita entiende ese ver como reconocer la unidad; el Dvaita y el Vishishtadvaita, como volverse hacia un Señor distinto del ser.

stem: in the Chandogya Upanishad (chapter 7), Narada has learned the Vedas and many sciences, yet comes to Sanatkumara in sorrow. what does Sanatkumara say all that learning is, and where does his teaching lead?
why: Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.3 calls Narada's learning "only name" and says the knower of the self crosses beyond sorrow; 7.23 says "the infinite (bhuman) is happiness; there is no happiness in the small."

rubric.point: says Sanatkumara calls that learning "only name" (nama), so it does not carry Narada beyond sorrow. saying the learning is false or worthless does not count.
says the teaching climbs step by step (name, speech, mind and onward) up to bhuman, the infinite.
says the infinite alone is happiness, with no happiness in the small, or that the knower of the self crosses beyond sorrow.
gives the mark of the infinite: where one sees, hears and understands nothing else (7.24).

es.stem: en la Chandogya Upanishad (capítulo 7), Narada ha aprendido los Vedas y muchas ciencias, pero llega donde Sanatkumara lleno de tristeza. ¿qué dice Sanatkumara que es todo ese saber, y adónde lleva su enseñanza?
es.why: Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.3 llama al saber de Narada "solo nombre" y dice que quien conoce el ser cruza más allá de la tristeza; 7.23 dice "lo infinito (bhuman) es felicidad; no hay felicidad en lo pequeño".
